## Charter

# CHARTER — Off-Peak Fare Capping at Riverton Transit Authority: A Briefing Note

## Deliverable
What: A briefing note to the Riverton Transit Authority (RTA) Board of
Directors evaluating whether RTA should adopt an off-peak fare cap, and
recommending how. Through-line: RTA should adopt an off-peak fare cap
through a phased, corridor-first pilot, because peer-agency evidence shows
off-peak capping grows ridership without a full-fare-equivalent revenue
loss, and RTA's own ridership and equity data show the riders most
underserved by its current all-day cap are exactly the riders concentrated
in the off-peak window.
Format: markdown, rendered last via the format skill
Total size: 4200w, 5items
(body sections only, B002-B006; the executive summary is front-matter.md and
the conclusion/recommendation is back-matter.md, written by hand in the seam
pass — see PLAN.md and WALKTHROUGH.md — and are not separately budgeted plan
units)

## Audience
The RTA Board of Directors and the General Manager's senior staff. They know
RTA's network and current fare structure well; they do not have the peer-
agency data, the fare-system technical constraints, or the equity office's
analysis in front of them, and this note is their first consolidated look at
all three together ahead of a vote on whether to direct staff to proceed.

## Voice & register
Third person, board-briefing register: precise, plain, comfortable citing
figures, and willing to name a tradeoff without hiding it. No first person,
no rhetorical questions, and no recommendation stated as settled until the
conclusion — body sections lay out evidence and tradeoffs, not verdicts.

## Non-negotiables
1. Every ridership, revenue, cost, or date figure carries a [S#] source tag
   traceable to a file in Sources of truth.
2. The terminology lock is followed exactly; no synonyms for locked terms.
3. The implementation options section presents at least two options as
   options the Board could choose among, never as a decision already made.
4. Equity implications for low-income riders are addressed as their own
   subject, not folded into a general accessibility statement.
5. No section before the conclusion states outright that RTA should adopt
   an off-peak cap; sections build the evidence, the conclusion states the
   recommendation.

### sources/peer-program-outcomes.md

# Source memo — Off-peak fare capping: three peer-agency outcomes

Prepared by RTA Strategy & Planning, compiled from peer-agency public board
reports and direct agency-to-agency data requests, 2026-08. Three mid-size
agencies with comparable service area and fleet size to Riverton Transit
Authority (RTA) have implemented some form of off-peak fare capping. Figures
below are as each agency reported them; none have been independently audited
by RTA.

## Meridian Transit (population served ~310,000)

Launched a system-wide off-peak fare cap in March 2023: riders who tap 6 times
between 9:00 a.m.-3:00 p.m. or after 7:00 p.m. on a service day pay nothing
further that day, versus a 12-tap cap for peak-period riders. Meridian
reports off-peak boardings rose 11% in the twelve months after launch,
against 2% system-wide growth in the same window. Off-peak fare revenue per
boarding fell 9%, but total off-peak revenue rose 4% on the higher volume.
Meridian's finance office attributes most of the ridership gain to riders who
previously avoided a second midday trip once they had already paid a peak
fare that morning. Implementation cost was $340,000 in fare-system software
changes and took 7 months from board approval to launch. Meridian did not
change its fare enforcement or verification process; the cap is applied
automatically by its account-based fare system.

## Cedar Falls Regional Transit (population served ~265,000)

Launched an off-peak cap in September 2022, restricted to riders enrolled in
its reduced-fare program (seniors, riders with disabilities, and
income-qualified riders). Enrolled off-peak riders pay a flat $0.75 per
boarding after their second off-peak tap in a day, down from a per-boarding
fare of $1.25. Cedar Falls reports enrolled-rider off-peak boardings rose 18%
in the first year, and cites exit-survey data showing 61% of enrolled riders
who increased off-peak travel cited the cap as the reason. Because the
program targeted only enrolled riders, total system revenue impact was small:
a 0.6% reduction in system-wide fare revenue. Cedar Falls' technology cost was
lower, $95,000, because the cap only had to be evaluated against one rider
class already flagged in the fare system; the tradeoff its board minutes note
explicitly is that non-enrolled low-income riders who have not completed
reduced-fare enrollment see no benefit at all.

## Ashford Regional Transit (population served ~220,000)

Ran a 14-month pilot, March 2024 through May 2025, on a single high-ridership
corridor rather than system-wide, capping off-peak boardings at 4 taps per
day on that corridor only. Ashford reports corridor off-peak ridership rose
7%, a smaller gain than Meridian's system-wide result, which Ashford's
after-action report attributes to the pilot's single-corridor scope limiting
awareness — only 34% of surveyed riders on the corridor knew the cap existed
by month 6. Ashford's pilot cost $110,000 and took 5 months to stand up
because it reused existing fare-system logic rather than building new
account-based capping. Ashford's board voted in June 2025 to expand the cap
system-wide starting in 2027, citing the pilot's ridership gain as sufficient
evidence despite the low awareness rate.

## Cross-agency notes

All three agencies report that off-peak fare capping produced a ridership
gain without producing a full-fare-equivalent revenue loss, because the
riders responding to the cap were largely riders who would otherwise have
made zero or one off-peak trip, not riders substituting away from an
already-paid peak fare. None of the three agencies reported measurable
change in vehicle crowding or added service costs from the added off-peak
ridership; all three had spare off-peak capacity before launch. Meridian and
Cedar Falls both used their existing account-based (tap-and-cap) fare
systems with a software change; Ashford's corridor-only approach was a
lower-cost, lower-awareness path that its own board later judged
insufficient. No agency in this set reported a labor-relations dispute tied
to the fare change itself, though Meridian's operator union did request (and
receive) six weeks of advance notice before the fare change took effect on
vehicles.

### sources/riverton-ridership-data.md

# Data memo — RTA ridership and fare revenue by time period

Prepared by RTA Planning & Scheduling from the FY2026 automated fare
collection (AFC) extract and the FY2026 operating budget. Figures cover
Riverton Transit Authority's fixed-route bus and light-rail network only;
paratransit (RTA Access) is reported separately in the stakeholder notes.

## System totals, FY2026

RTA recorded 21.4 million unweighted boardings in FY2026, up 1.8% from
FY2025. Fixed-route fare revenue was $28.6 million. RTA's existing fare
product is a single all-day cap: a rider pays full fare for their first 2
taps in a service day (6:00 a.m.-11:59 p.m.) and rides free the rest of that
day, regardless of when those first 2 taps occur. This all-day cap has been
in place since 2019 and is not time-of-day differentiated.

## Boardings and revenue by day-part

RTA's AFC system buckets boardings into three day-parts: AM peak (6:00-9:30
a.m.), midday/PM peak combined as "daytime" (9:30 a.m.-6:30 p.m., which
includes the 4:00-6:30 p.m. PM peak), and off-peak (6:30 p.m.-11:59 p.m. plus
all weekend hours). For FY2026:

- AM peak: 6.2 million boardings (29% of system total), $9.1 million revenue.
- Daytime (including PM peak): 10.5 million boardings (49% of system total),
  $13.8 million revenue.
- Off-peak (evenings and weekends): 4.7 million boardings (22% of system
  total), $5.7 million revenue.

Average fare revenue per boarding is therefore highest in AM peak ($1.47)
and lowest off-peak ($1.21), consistent with the existing all-day cap: a
rider who taps twice in the morning rush already rides free for the rest of
the day, including any off-peak trips, so off-peak boardings by cap-covered
riders generate no incremental revenue at all. RTA Planning estimates 38% of
off-peak boardings are made by riders who already reached the all-day cap
earlier that same day; the remaining 62% are riders making an off-peak-only
trip (a single fare, no cap benefit) or a second trip on a day when their
first trip was also off-peak.

## Growth and capacity

Off-peak ridership grew 3.1% year over year, faster than the 1.8% system
average, driven mostly by evening service on the two light-rail lines. RTA's
fleet utilization data shows off-peak trips run at 34% average seat
occupancy system-wide, compared with 78% in AM peak and 71% in PM peak — RTA
has substantial unused off-peak capacity on nearly every route. No route in
the FY2026 schedule is capacity-constrained off-peak.

## Prior fare-change history

RTA's board last changed the base fare in 2021 (a $0.15 increase) and
introduced the current all-day cap in 2019. Both changes went through a
90-day public comment period under RTA's fare-change policy. RTA has not
previously implemented a fare product differentiated by time of day; the
all-day cap is uniform regardless of when a rider's first two taps occur.

### sources/farebox-tech-memo.md

# Technical memo — RiverPass fare system capability for time-of-day capping

Prepared by RTA IT/Fare Systems, 2026-07, in response to a Planning
department request to scope what a time-of-day (off-peak-specific) fare cap
would require of the existing fare system.

## Current system

RTA's fare system, branded RiverPass, is an account-based tap card and phone
app installed in 2020 and last upgraded in 2023. Fare validation at the
farebox is real-time (a tap is authorized or declined in under one second),
but cap accounting — deciding whether a rider has reached a cap and should
ride free — currently runs as a nightly batch job, not in real time. In
practice this means a rider who has already reached the all-day cap can still
be charged at the farebox for a tap that happens later the same day; RTA
credits the overcharge back to the rider's account the following morning
once the batch job runs. RTA data shows roughly 4% of all-day-cap-eligible
taps are overcharged and refunded this way in an average week.

## What a time-of-day cap would require

A cap that behaves differently depending on the time of the tap (for
example, a lower or zero fare after a rider's second off-peak tap, while
still charging peak fare the same day) cannot be evaluated correctly by the
current nightly batch process, because the batch job does not know at tap
time whether a given tap falls inside or outside the off-peak window relative
to the rider's other taps that day — it only reconciles cumulative daily
taps after the fact. RiverPass would need a software change to move cap
evaluation into the real-time authorization path so that the farebox knows,
at the moment of the tap, both the time of day and the rider's cap status.

RTA's fare-system vendor quoted this change at $410,000 and a 9-month
delivery timeline from contract signature, based on a scoping call in June
2026; the quote has not been through RTA procurement review and is not a
binding bid. The 9 months includes 2 months of vendor development, 3 months
of RTA-side integration testing against the existing farebox hardware
(unchanged since 2020), and a recommended 4-month phased rollout across
RTA's approximately 340 buses and 22 light-rail vehicles rather than a single
cutover, to catch hardware-specific validation bugs before they affect the
whole fleet.

## Interim option

RTA's fare-system vendor also described a lower-cost interim path: keep cap
evaluation in the nightly batch job, but change only the refund logic so
that any rider whose batch reconciliation shows they qualified for an
off-peak cap that day receives an automatic same-week account credit rather
than riding free at the farebox in real time. This interim option was quoted
at $85,000 and 3 months, because it changes only the batch job's refund
rule, not the real-time authorization path. Its tradeoff, as the vendor's
scoping notes state directly, is that a rider does not experience "riding
free" at the point of travel — they pay full fare at the farebox and see the
credit on their account days later, which RTA's own product staff flagged in
the scoping call as a meaningfully worse rider experience than real-time
capping, even though the two options are intended to produce the same net
fare outcome.

## Hardware note

The farebox hardware itself (installed 2020) supports both paths without
replacement; the vendor's quote in both cases is software-only. RTA's IT
department has no other planned RiverPass changes competing for 2027
engineering capacity as of this memo's writing.

### sources/equity-analysis-notes.md

# Equity office analysis notes — off-peak ridership and low-income riders

Prepared by RTA's Equity & Access office, 2026-08, using FY2026 reduced-fare
program enrollment as a proxy for low-income ridership (RTA does not collect
rider income directly; reduced-fare enrollment requires documented enrollment
in one of four qualifying income-based assistance programs).

## Enrollment and travel pattern

RTA's reduced-fare program has 41,000 enrolled riders as of FY2026. Enrolled
riders account for 19% of system-wide boardings but 33% of off-peak
boardings — reduced-fare riders are roughly twice as likely, proportionally,
to be traveling off-peak as the ridership base overall. The Equity office's
working explanation, drawn from a FY2025 rider survey, is that enrolled
riders disproportionately work evening, overnight, or weekend shifts in
retail, food service, and healthcare support roles, and disproportionately
make non-work trips (grocery, medical, childcare pickup) outside the
traditional 9-to-5 travel window that the current all-day cap was designed
around.

## Why the current all-day cap underserves this group

Because RTA's existing all-day cap only pays off once a rider has already
taken 2 taps that day, it mechanically benefits multi-trip peak-anchored
travel most: a rider who commutes in and out during peak hours reaches the
cap on their commute alone and then rides free the rest of the day, including
any off-peak trips. A rider whose only trips that day are off-peak — the
pattern the Equity office's survey associates most with enrolled reduced-fare
riders — pays full fare for both taps and never reaches the cap at all. The
Equity office's analysis states plainly that the current fare structure's
largest cap benefit accrues to peak commuters, not to the reduced-fare
population the program exists to serve.

## Geographic concentration

Reduced-fare enrollment is concentrated in four of RTA's twelve service
corridors (the Eastside, Harbor, Millbrook, and Southgate corridors), which
together account for 58% of all enrolled riders despite carrying 31% of
system-wide boardings. All four of these corridors also appear in RTA's
off-peak ridership growth data as above-average growth corridors over the
past two years. The Equity office notes this overlap as suggestive, not
proven: it has not run a corridor-level regression isolating the reduced-fare
population's contribution to each corridor's off-peak growth.

## What an off-peak cap could change

An off-peak-specific cap — one that pays off after fewer taps than the
current all-day cap, but only for taps in the off-peak window — would create
a path to fare relief for a rider whose only travel that day is off-peak,
which the current structure does not. The Equity office's preliminary
estimate, based on applying Meridian Transit's reported 11% off-peak
ridership response to RTA's reduced-fare-heavy corridors only, is that
enrolled riders in the four highest-concentration corridors could see
off-peak trip costs fall by an amount comparable to Cedar Falls Regional
Transit's reported outcome for its enrolled population, though the Equity
office is explicit that this is an extrapolation from two peer agencies, not
a Riverton-specific model.

## Caution the office asked to be carried forward

The Equity office's notes ask explicitly that any proposal be evaluated
against whether it also serves non-enrolled low-income riders — people who
would qualify for reduced fare but have not completed enrollment — since a
cap benefit tied only to enrollment status would miss a share of the
population the equity goal is meant to reach; the office did not estimate
the size of that unenrolled-but-eligible group in this analysis.

### sources/stakeholder-interview-notes.md

# Stakeholder interview notes — off-peak fare cap proposal

Compiled by RTA Planning from three interviews conducted 2026-08 as part of
scoping an off-peak fare cap proposal. Notes are summarized from recordings
with each interviewee's consent; quotes are lightly edited for length.

## Amalgamated Transit Operators Local 219 (driver union), interview 2026-08-11

Interviewed: union grievance officer and one shop steward. The union's
primary concern was fare enforcement during any transition period, not the
policy itself. Quote: "Every time fare rules change, drivers are the ones
riders argue with at the farebox until the system catches up. Give us
written guidance and enough lead time before the change hits the road." The
union asked for a minimum 60-day advance notice before any fare change takes
effect on vehicles, citing Meridian Transit's six-week notice as a floor, not
a ceiling, given RTA's larger fleet. The union did not oppose an off-peak cap
in principle and noted that reduced disputes over an already-reached cap
(riders arguing they should ride free) would, if anything, reduce
farebox-adjacent conflict during off-peak shifts, which the union's members
generally staff.

## RTA Access (paratransit office), interview 2026-08-13

Interviewed: RTA Access program manager. RTA Access, the agency's paratransit
service, operates under a separate fare schedule (currently a flat $2.50 per
trip, not subject to the fixed-route all-day cap) and the program manager
was clear that any fixed-route off-peak cap should not be assumed to apply to
Access trips without a separate board action, since Access is funded and
budgeted on a distinct formula tied to ADA paratransit complementary-service
requirements. The program manager flagged one adjacent concern: if an
off-peak fixed-route cap meaningfully increases off-peak fixed-route
ridership among riders who currently use Access because fixed-route service
feels financially unpredictable off-peak, Access could see a small ridership
shift onto fixed-route, which the office would view as a positive outcome
for program cost but asked to be consulted before any public communication
implies Access riders are a target population for the fixed-route change.

## RTA Finance office, interview 2026-08-14

Interviewed: deputy CFO. Finance's central concern was cash-flow timing
under the real-time-capping option described in the fare-system technical
memo: a $410,000 up-front technology cost against a revenue effect that, per
Finance's read of the peer-agency data, is likely to be revenue-neutral to
modestly positive within a year but is not free in year one. The deputy CFO
was explicit that the office does not oppose the concept and thinks a phased
rollout, starting on RTA's highest reduced-fare-concentration corridors
before a system-wide expansion, is "the fiscally disciplined way to test the
revenue assumption before committing the full technology spend" — closer to
Ashford Regional Transit's corridor-first approach than to Meridian's
system-wide launch, though Finance also flagged that Ashford's low
rider-awareness result (only about a third of riders knew the cap existed by
month six) is a communication failure worth designing around, not a reason
to avoid a phased approach. Finance asked that any board memo distinguish
clearly between the $410,000 real-time option and the $85,000 interim
batch-credit option, since the two have materially different cash-flow and
procurement timelines.
